blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Periodic Motion :-

Any motion which repeats itself after regular interval of time is called periodic motion.

Oscillatory Motion:

The motion of a body is said to be oscillatory or vibratory motion if it moves back and forth (to and fro) about a fixed point. Example: Oscillations of the mass attached from spring.

SHM Basic Terms

(1) One Oscillation or Vibration: When a particle goes to one side from mean position and returns back and then it goes to other side and again returns back to mean position, then this process is known as one oscillation.

(2) Mean Position :- The point at which the restoring force on the particle is zero and potential energy is minimum.

(3) Restoring Force :- The force acting on the particle which tends to bring the particle towards its mean position, is known as restoring force.

(4) Amplitude (A) :- The maximum displacement of particle from mean position is define as amplitude.

(5) Time period (T) :- : The minimum time after which the particle keeps on repeating its motion is known as time period. or time taken to Complete one oscillation.

$T = \dfrac{1}{n}$ ,   $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}
$

(6) Frequency (n or f) :The number of oscillations per second is defined as frequency. The SI Unit is Hertz(Hz)

$f = \dfrac{1}{T}$ ,     $f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$

(7) Angular frequency ($\omega$) :-The rate of change of phase angle of a particle with respect to time.SI unit Radian/Second

Note :-  In one oscillation Distance travelled = 4A , Displacement = 0 , Length of line of SHM = 2A

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: What is oscillatory motion?
blocks.answer: Oscillatory motion refers to a type of repetitive back-and-forth movement about a fixed point.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: Can you think of examples of motions that repeat regularly but might not be considered periodic? What distinguishes them?
blocks.answer: Imagine a car driving around a circular track, but the driver sometimes speeds up and sometimes slows down. The car's path repeats, but the time it takes to complete each lap is different. This is not periodic motion. Another example is a heartbeat that occasionally skips a beat or has extra beats. The pattern repeats roughly, but the intervals aren't consistent.
blocks.prompt: Can you think of examples of motions that repeat regularly but might not be considered periodic? What distinguishes them?

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing amplitude with frequency or period.
  • Assuming oscillations always occur at a constant speed.
  • Ignoring the effect of damping or friction in real oscillatory systems.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Necessary Conditions to execute S.H.M.

• Motion of particle should be oscillatory.
        • Total mechanical energy of particle should be conserved (Kinetic energy + Potential energy = constant)
        • Extreme position should be well defined.
• In linear S.H.M the restoring force (or acceleration) acting on the particle should always be proportional to the displacement of the particle and directed towards the equilibrium position.

$F \propto -x \quad \text{or} \quad a \propto -x$

( Negative sign shows that direction of force and acceleration is towards equilibrium position and x is displacement of particle from equilibrium position).

• In angular S.H.M. the restoring torque (or angular acceleration) acting on the particle should always be proportional to the angular displacement of the particle and directed towards the equilibrium position.

$\tau \propto -\theta \quad \text{or} \quad \alpha \propto -\theta$

Linear SHM :When a particle moves to and fro about a fixed point (called equilibrium position) along a straight line.

Example : Motion of a mass connected to spring$$

$F = -kx$, where k is the spring constant and x is the displacement from mean position.

$a = -\dfrac{k}{m} x \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \dfrac{k}{m} x = 0$

$x = A \sin(\omega t)$

$a = -\omega^2 x$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{k}{m}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$

Angular S.H.M:  When a system oscillates angularly with respect to a fixed axis then its motion is called angular simple harmonic motion.

Example :- Motion of a bob of simple pendulum

$\tau \propto -\theta \quad \Rightarrow \quad \tau = -C\theta$

$\alpha = -\dfrac{C}{I} \theta \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \dfrac{C}{I} \theta = 0$

$\theta = \theta_0 \sin(\omega t) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \alpha = -\omega^2 \theta$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{C}{I}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{C}}$

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{C}{I}}$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Check whether the given function represents SHM or not.

$y = \sin(\omega t) + 2 \cos(\omega t)$
blocks.answer:
$v = \frac{dy}{dt} = \omega \cos(\omega t) - 2\omega \sin(\omega t)$

$a = \frac{dv}{dt} = -\omega^2 \sin(\omega t) - 2 \omega^2 \cos(\omega t) = -\omega^2 \left( \sin(\omega t) + 2 \cos(\omega t) \right) = -\omega^2 y$

The given function represents SHM.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Geometrical meaning of S.H.M: If a particle is moving with uniform speed along the circumference of a circle then the straight line motion of the foot of perpendicular drawn from the particle on the diameter of the circle is called S.H.M.

Displacement in SHM:

$x = A \sin(\omega t)$ or $x = A \cos(\omega t)$

Maximum value of displacement is = ± A

Velocity in S.H.M.: It is defined as the time rate of change of the displacement of the particle at a given instant.

$\text { if } x=A \sin \omega t$

$v = A \omega \cos(\omega t)$

$v = \pm \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$

$\dfrac{x^2}{A^2} + \dfrac{v^2}{A^2 \omega^2} = 1$

This is equation of ellipse. So, curve between displacement and velocity of particle executing S.H.M. is ellipse.  If particle oscillates with unit angular frequency then curve between V and x will be circle.

Note

    • The direction of velocity of a particle in S.H.M. is either towards or away from the mean position.

• At mean position ($x=0$), velocity is maximum $v_{\text{max}} = \pm A \omega$ and at extreme position $x = \pm A$, the velocity of particle executing S.H.M. is zero.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: The radius of the circle, the period of revolution, the initial position and the sense of revolution are indicated in the figures. Obtain the simple harmonic motions of the x-projection of the radius vector of the rotating particle P.
blocks.answer:
At t = 0, OP makes an angle of 45° = $\frac{\pi}{4}$ with the (positive direction of) x-axis. After time t, it covers an $\frac{2\pi}{T} t$ in  the anticlockwise sense, and makes an angle of $\frac{2\pi}{T} t + \frac{\pi}{4}$with the x-axis. The projection of OP on the x-axis at time t is given by,

$x(t) = A \cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{T} t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)$

For$   T = 4 s,$$x(t) = A \cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{4} t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ OR  $x(t)=A \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2} t+\pi / 4\right)$

which is a SHM of amplitude $A$, period $4s$, and an initial phase =$\frac{\pi}{4}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Thinking SHM is the same as circular motion itself, not its projection.
  • Confusing the radius of the circle with the displacement at all times.
  • Ignoring that the projection oscillates back and forth along a straight line, not around the circle.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Acceleration in S.H.M: It is defined as the time rate of change of the velocity of the particle at given instant.

if $x=A \sin \omega t$ Then $a=-\omega^2 A \sin \omega t$

$a = -\omega^2 x$

  • The graph between acceleration and displacement is straight line.
  • Relation between force(F) and time(t) $F = ma = -m \omega^2 A \sin(\omega t)$
Relation between force(F) and displacement(x) is $F = -m \omega^2 x$

Note:

(1)The acceleration of a particle executing S.H.M. is always directed towards the mean position.

(2) The acceleration of the particle executing S.H.M. is maximum at extreme position ($\pm \omega^2 A$) and minimum at mean position (= zero).

(3) Maximum value of acceleration is $\pm \omega^2 A$

(4) Maximum value of force is $\pm m \omega^2 A$

Key Points

Velocity and acceleration of particle in SHM :-

Displacement:
$x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi)$
$$Velocity:
$v(t) = -A \omega \sin(\omega t + \phi)$

$v = \pm \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$  (Velocity in terms of displacement)

(i) at x = 0 (mean position)     $v_{\text{max}} =\pm \omega A$

(ii) at extreme position ($x = \pm A$)      $v_{\text{min}} = 0$$$

Acceleration:
$a(t) = -A \omega^2 \cos(\omega t + \phi)$

$a = -\omega^2 x$   (Acceleration in terms of displacement)

(i) at x = 0 (Mean position)  $a_{\text{min}} = 0$

(ii) at Extreme position   ($x = \pm A$)    $a = \pm \omega^2 A$

Phase difference between x, v and a :

  • (i) displacement and velocity = $\frac{\pi}{2}$
  • (ii) velocity and acceleration =$\frac{\pi}{2}$
  • (iii) displacement and acceleration = $\pi
$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
An object performs S.H.M. of amplitude 5 cm and time period 4 s. If timing is started when the object is at the centre of the oscillation i.e. x = 0 then calculate

(1)Frequency of oscillation

(2)The displacement at 0.5 sec.

(3)The maximum acceleration of the object.

(4)The velocity at a displacement of 3 cm.
blocks.answer:
(1)Frequency

$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25 \, \text{Hz}$

(2)The displacement equation of object $x = A \sin(\omega t)$

so at $t = 0.5 s$

$x = 5 \sin\left(2\pi \times 0.25 \times 0.5\right) = 5 \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}$ cm

(3) Maximum acceleration

$a_{\text{max}} = \omega^2 A = \left( 0.5 \pi \right)^2 \times 5 = 12.3 \, \text{cm/s}^2$

(4) Velocity at $ x = 3 cm$ is

$v = \pm \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = \pm 0.5 \pi \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \pm 6.28 \, \text{cm/s}$
options: (4)The velocity at a displacement of 3 cm.

blocks.question: A particle executing S.H.M. having amplitude 0.01 m and frequency 60 Hz. Determine maximum acceleration of particle.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Thinking acceleration is constant throughout the motion.
  • Assuming acceleration is in the direction of motion (velocity).
  • Ignoring that acceleration is always directed towards the mean (equilibrium) position and proportional to displacement.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Potential Energy in S.H.M.

(1) In terms of displacement

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 + C$

$\text{At } x = 0, \, U = U_0 \Rightarrow C = U_0 \quad \text{So,} \quad U =\dfrac{1}{2} kx^2 + U_0$

Where the potential energy at equilibrium position = $U_0$

when $U_0 = 0$ then $U =\dfrac{1}{2} kx^2$

(2) In terms of time

$x = A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$

$U = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 \sin^2(\omega t + \phi)$

$\text{If initial phase } (\phi) \text{ is zero, then} \quad U = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 \sin^2(\omega t) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \sin^2(\omega t)$

Note:

In S.H.M. the potential energy is a parabolic function of displacement; the potential energy is minimum$\left(u=v_0\right)$ at the mean position $(x = 0)$ and maximum $(U=\frac{1}{2} k A^2+U_0)$ at extreme position $(x = \pm A)$

Kinetic Energy$(K.E.)$

(1) In terms of displacement

$\text{K.E.} = \dfrac{1}{2} mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} k (A^2 - x^2)$

(2) In terms of time

$ \text{K.E.} = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \cos^2(\omega t + \phi)$

$\text{If initial phase } \phi = 0, \quad \text{K.E.} = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \cos^2(\omega t)$

Note:

In S.H.M. the kinetic energy is a inverted parabolic function of displacement; the kinetic energy is maximum($\frac{1}{2} k A^2)$ at the mean position $(x = 0)$ and minimum (zero) at extreme position $(x = \pm A)$

Total Energy in SHM and Graphs

Total energy in S.H.M. is given by :-

E = potential energy + kinetic energy = U + K.E

(1)  w.r.t Position:

$E = \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 = \text{Constant}$

(2) w.r.t Time

$ E = \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 = \text{Constant}$

Note:

(1)Total energy of a particle in S.H.M. is same at all instant and at all displacement.

(2)Total energy depends upon mass, amplitude and frequency of vibration of the particle executing S.H.M.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A particle starts oscillating simple harmonically from its equilibrium position with time period $T.$Determine ratio of K.E. and P.E. of the particle at time $t=$$\frac{T}{12}$.
blocks.answer:
$\text{at } t = \frac{T}{12}$

$x = A \sin\left( \frac{2\pi}{T} \times \frac{T}{12} \right) = A \sin\left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) = \frac{A}{2}$

So,$\text{K.E.} = \frac{1}{2} k \left( A^2 - x^2 \right) = \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} k A^2$

$\text{P.E.} = \frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} k A^2$

$\frac{\text{K.E.}}{\text{P.E.}} = \frac{3}{1}$
blocks.prompt: A particle starts oscillating simple harmonically from its equilibrium position with time period $T.$Determine ratio of K.E. and P.E. of the particle at time $t=$$\frac{T}{12}$.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: A harmonic oscillator of force constant 4 × 106 Nm–1 and amplitude 0.01 m has total energy 240 J. What is maximum kinetic energy and minimum potential energy?
blocks.answer:
$k = 4 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/m}$,$\quad A = 0.01 \, \text{m}$,

$T.E=240J$

$\omega^2 = \frac{k}{m}$

Maximum Kinetic Energy=$\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 10^6 \times (0.01)^2 = 200 \, \text{J}$

Minimum potential energy=Total energy-maximum kinetic energy=$40 J$
blocks.prompt: A harmonic oscillator of force constant 4 × 106 Nm–1 and amplitude 0.01 m has total energy 240 J. What is maximum kinetic energy and minimum potential energy?

blocks.title: Example-3
blocks.question: A particle is vibrating in a simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 4 cm. At what displacement from the equilibrium position, its energy is half potential and half kinetic.
blocks.answer:
Let  $x$ be the point where $K.E=P.E$

$\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 2 x^2 = A^2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = \pm 2 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~cm} $
blocks.prompt: A particle is vibrating in a simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 4 cm. At what displacement from the equilibrium position, its energy is half potential and half kinetic.

blocks.text:
• Assuming kinetic energy is maximum at extreme positions
  • Forgetting that total energy is proportional to the square of amplitude

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
(1) Spring Block System

(1) When spring is given small displacement by stretching or compressing it, then restoring elastic force is developed in it which obeys Hook's law.

$F \propto -x \quad \Rightarrow \quad F = -kx$ (Here $k$ is a spring constant)

(2) Spring is assumed massless, so restoring elastic force in spring is assumed same everywhere

(3) Spring constant $(k) $depends on length $(l),$radius and material of wire used in spring.

For spring,$ kl = constant$

(2) Spring Pendulum : When a small mass is suspended from a mass-less spring then this arrangement is known as spring pendulum. For small linear displacement the motion of spring pendulum is simple harmonic.

(i) Time-Period

$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

(ii) Frequency

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$

(3) Time period of a spring pendulum is independent of acceleration due to gravity. This is why a clock based on oscillation of spring pendulum will keep proper time everywhere on a hill or moon or in a satellite or different places of earth.

(4) If a spring pendulum oscillates in a vertical plane is made to oscillate on a horizontal surface or on an inclined plane then time period will remain unchanged.

(5) By increasing the mass, time period of spring pendulum increases $(T \propto \sqrt{m})$ , but by increasing the force constant of spring$ (k)$,Its time period decreases $T \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{k}}$

whereas frequency increases $f \propto \sqrt{k}$

(6) If two masses m1 and m2 are connected by a spring and made to oscillate then time period $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu}{k}}$  Here $\mu = \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$= reduced mass

(7) If the stretch in a vertically loaded spring is y0 then for equilibrium of mass m.

$k y_0 = mg$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{y_0

}{g}}$

But remember time period of spring pendulum is independent of acceleration due to gravity.

(8) If two particles are attached with spring in which only one is oscillating then the

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m_1}{k}}$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A block of mass m is attached from a spring of spring constant k and dropped from its natural length. Find the amplitude of S.H.M.
blocks.answer:
Let amplitude of S.H.M be $ A$ then by work energy theorem

$W = \Delta K.E$

$mgx_0 - \dfrac{1}{2}kx_0^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x_0 = \dfrac{2mg}{k}$

So, Amplitude  $A = \dfrac{mg}{k}$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: A block of mass m is on a horizontal slab of mass M which is moving horizontally and executing S.H.M. The coefficient of static friction between block and slab is µ. If block is not separated from slab then determine angular frequency of oscillation.
blocks.answer:
If block is not separated from slab then restoring force due to S.H.M. should be less than frictional force between slab and block

$F_{\text{restoring}} \leq F_{\text{friction}} \rightarrow m a_{\text{max}} \leq \mu mg \rightarrow a_{\text{max}} \leq \mu g \rightarrow \omega^2 A \leq \mu g \Rightarrow \omega \leq \sqrt{\frac{\mu g}{A}}$
blocks.prompt: A block of mass m is on a horizontal slab of mass M which is moving horizontally and executing S.H.M. The coefficient of static friction between block and slab is µ. If block is not separated from slab then determine angular frequency of oscillation.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Series Combination of Springs: In series combination same restoring force exerts in all springs but extension will be different.

Time Period(T): $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_s}}$

Frequency(n):$n = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k_s}{m}}$

Angular Frequency($\omega$) :$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_s}{m}}$

$k_s = \dfrac{k_1 k_2}{k_1 + k_2}$

$\text { for } n \text { sprigs } \frac{1}{k_s}=\frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}+\frac{1}{k_3}+\cdots+\frac{1}{k_n}$

Parallel Combination of Springs: In parallel combination displacement on each spring is same but restoring force is different

Time Period(T):

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_{p}}}$

Frequency(n): $n = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k_p}{m}}$

Angular Frequency $(\omega)$: $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_p}{m}}$

$k_p = k_1 + k_2$

$\text { for } n \text { sprigs } k_p=k_1+k_2+k_3+\ldots$

modules.name: Simple Pendulum and Its Various Cases

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Simple Pendulum: If a heavy point mass is suspended by a weightless, inextensible and perfectly flexible string from a rigid support, then this arrangement is called a simple pendulum.$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$

Cases of Effective Acceleration in Simple Pendulum

Periodic time of simple pendulum in reference system

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}}$

$g_{\text{eff}} = $ effective gravitational acceleration in reference system (or total downward acceleration)

(a) If reference system is lift

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}} \quad \text{where} \quad g_{\text{eff}} = g \quad \text{when velocity of lift} \ (v) = \text{constant}, \ a = 0$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$

(b) If Lift is accelerating upwards

$g_{\text{eff}} = g + a$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g + a}}$

$T$$\Rightarrow$ Decreases

(c) If Lift is accelerating Downwards

$g_{\text{eff}} = g - a$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g - a}}$

$T$$\Rightarrow$ Increases

(d) If lift falls downwards freely

$g_{\text{eff}} = g - g$

$T=$$\infty$

simple pendulum will not oscillate.

Note: If simple pendulum is shifted to the centre of earth, freely falling lift, in artificial satellite then it will not oscillate and its time period is infinite ( geff. = 0).

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: The period of a simple pendulum measured inside a stationary lift is found to be T. If the lift starts accelerating upwards with acceleration of g/3 then the time period of the pendulum is ?
blocks.answer:
For stationary lift

$T_1 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$

For ascending lift with acceleration $a$

$T_2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g + a}}$

$\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \sqrt{\frac{g + a}{g}}$

$\frac{T_1}{T_2}=$$\sqrt{\frac{g + \frac{g}{3}}{g}}$

$\frac{T_1}{T_2}=$$\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}$

$\frac{T_1}{T_2}={\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}}$

$T_2 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} T$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: If the length of the simple pendulum is increased by 44%, then what is the change in time period of pendulum?

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Assuming motion is SHM for all amplitudes
  • Ignoring the effect of length on time period
  • Mistaking mass of the bob affects time period

blocks.title: Core concept
blocks.text:
A simple pendulum is mounted on a moving truck

• If truck is moving with constant velocity, no pseudo force acts on the pendulum and time period remains same.

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$

• If truck accelerates forward with acceleration 'a' then a pseudo force acts in opposite direction.

$T' = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{\sqrt{g^2 + a^2}}}$

$T'$$\Rightarrow$ decreases.

• If a simple pendulum of density $\sigma$ is made to oscillate in a liquid of density $\rho$ then its time period will increase as compare to that of air and is given by

$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{\left[1-\dfrac{\rho}{\sigma}\right] g}}$

• If the bob of simple pendulum has positive charge q and pendulum is placed in uniform electric field which is in downward direction then time period decreases

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g + \dfrac{qE}{m}}}$

• If the bob of simple pendulum has positive charge q and is made oscillate in uniform electric field acting in upward direction then time period increases

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g - \dfrac{qE}{m}}}$

When length of simple pendulum (l) is negligible as compare to radius of earth (l<< R) but if  is comparable to radius of earth

$ T=2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{\left[\dfrac{1}{\ell}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right] \mathrm{g}}}$

l = length of pendulum, R = radius of earth

• Second Pendulum :- On the surface of the Earth, the length of a second pendulum is approximately 1 metre and its time period is 2 seconds.

• When a long and short pendulum start oscillation simultaneously then both will be in same phase in minimum time when short pendulum complete one more oscillation compare to long pendulum.

$\mathrm{N} \sqrt{\ell_{\ell}}=(\mathrm{N}+1) \sqrt{l_{\mathrm{s}}}$

• If the bob of a simple pendulum is suspended by a metallic wire, and the wire has a linear expansion coefficient α, and the temperature changes by $d\theta$ then the effective length of the wire becomes  $l' = l \left( 1 + \alpha \, \Delta \theta \right)$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{T}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{T}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell^{\prime}}{\ell}}=(1+\alpha \mathrm{d} \theta)^{1 / 2}=1+\dfrac{1}{2} \alpha \mathrm{~d} \theta$

modules.name: Oscillations of General Bodies and Superposition of SHM

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
S.H.M. of a liquid in U tube: If a liquid of density r contained in a vertical U tube performs S.H.M. in its two limbs.

Time period=$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{h}{g}}$

S.H.M. of a floating cylinder : If a cylindrical object is floating in a liquid and is given a small displacement, i.e., slightly moved up and down, it performs a simple harmonic motion.

If $‘l’$ is the length of cylinder dipping in liquid then

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Time period }\\ &T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} \end{aligned}$

S.H.M. of a body in a tunnel dug along any chord of earth

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}$=$84.6    minutes$

Superposition of SHM: If particle is acted upon by two separate forces each of which can produce a SHM, the resultant motion of the particle is a combination of two SHM's.

$x_1 = A_1 \sin(\omega t), \quad x_2 = A_2 \sin(\omega t + \delta)$

$x = x_1 + x_2$

Amplitude of Resultant SHM

$A = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1 A_2 \cos(\delta)}$

$A_1$ and $A_2$ = Amplitude of Oscillations

$\omega $ = Angular Frequency

$\delta $ = Phase difference of both SHM

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question:
If two S.H.M. are represented by equations $y_1 = 10 \sin \left( 3\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)$ and

$y_2 = 5 [\sin(3\pi t) + \sqrt{3} \cos(3\pi t)]$,then find the ratio of their amplitudes and phase difference in between them.
blocks.answer:
$y_2 = 5 \sin(3\pi t) + 5 \sqrt{3} \cos(3\pi t)$...........(1)

$5 = A \cos(\phi) \quad \text{and} \quad 5\sqrt{3} = A \sin(\phi)$

$A = \sqrt{5^2 + (5\sqrt{3})^2} = 10$

$\tan(\phi) = \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{5} = \sqrt{3} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \phi = \frac{\pi}{3}$

the above equations(1) becomes

$y_2 = A \cos(\phi) \sin(3\pi t) + A \sin(\phi) \cos(3\pi t)$

$y_2 = A \sin(3\pi t + \phi)$

$y_2 = 10 \sin \left( 3\pi t + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)$

$\frac{A_1}{A_2} = \frac{10}{10} \implies \frac{A_1}{A_2} = 1:1$

Phase difference=$\frac{\pi}{3} - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{12} \, \text{rad}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Series Combination of Springs: In series combination same restoring force exerts in all springs but extension will be different.

Time Period(T): $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_s}}$

Frequency(n):$n = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k_s}{m}}$

Angular Frequency($\omega$) :$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_s}{m}}$

$k_s = \dfrac{k_1 k_2}{k_1 + k_2}$

$\text { for } n \text { sprigs } \frac{1}{k_s}=\frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}+\frac{1}{k_3}+\cdots+\frac{1}{k_n}$

Parallel Combination of Springs: In parallel combination displacement on each spring is same but restoring force is different

Time Period(T):

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_{p}}}$

Frequency(n): $n = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k_p}{m}}$

Angular Frequency $(\omega)$: $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_p}{m}}$

$k_p = k_1 + k_2$

$\text { for } n \text { sprigs } k_p=k_1+k_2+k_3+\ldots$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Necessary Conditions to execute S.H.M.

• Motion of particle should be oscillatory.
        • Total mechanical energy of particle should be conserved (Kinetic energy + Potential energy = constant)
        • Extreme position should be well defined.
• In linear S.H.M the restoring force (or acceleration) acting on the particle should always be proportional to the displacement of the particle and directed towards the equilibrium position.

$F \propto -x \quad \text{or} \quad a \propto -x$

( Negative sign shows that direction of force and acceleration is towards equilibrium position and x is displacement of particle from equilibrium position).

• In angular S.H.M. the restoring torque (or angular acceleration) acting on the particle should always be proportional to the angular displacement of the particle and directed towards the equilibrium position.

$\tau \propto -\theta \quad \text{or} \quad \alpha \propto -\theta$

Linear SHM :When a particle moves to and fro about a fixed point (called equilibrium position) along a straight line.

Example : Motion of a mass connected to spring$$

$F = -kx$, where k is the spring constant and x is the displacement from mean position.

$a = -\dfrac{k}{m} x \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \dfrac{k}{m} x = 0$

$x = A \sin(\omega t)$

$a = -\omega^2 x$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{k}{m}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$

Angular S.H.M:  When a system oscillates angularly with respect to a fixed axis then its motion is called angular simple harmonic motion.

Example :- Motion of a bob of simple pendulum

$\tau \propto -\theta \quad \Rightarrow \quad \tau = -C\theta$

$\alpha = -\dfrac{C}{I} \theta \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \dfrac{C}{I} \theta = 0$

$\theta = \theta_0 \sin(\omega t) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \alpha = -\omega^2 \theta$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{C}{I}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{C}}$

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{C}{I}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Geometrical meaning of S.H.M: If a particle is moving with uniform speed along the circumference of a circle then the straight line motion of the foot of perpendicular drawn from the particle on the diameter of the circle is called S.H.M.

Displacement in SHM:

$x = A \sin(\omega t)$ or $x = A \cos(\omega t)$

Maximum value of displacement is = ± A

Velocity in S.H.M.: It is defined as the time rate of change of the displacement of the particle at a given instant.

$\text { if } x=A \sin \omega t$

$v = A \omega \cos(\omega t)$

$v = \pm \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$

$\dfrac{x^2}{A^2} + \dfrac{v^2}{A^2 \omega^2} = 1$

This is equation of ellipse. So, curve between displacement and velocity of particle executing S.H.M. is ellipse.  If particle oscillates with unit angular frequency then curve between V and x will be circle.

Note

    • The direction of velocity of a particle in S.H.M. is either towards or away from the mean position.

• At mean position ($x=0$), velocity is maximum $v_{\text{max}} = \pm A \omega$ and at extreme position $x = \pm A$, the velocity of particle executing S.H.M. is zero.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Acceleration in S.H.M: It is defined as the time rate of change of the velocity of the particle at given instant.

if $x=A \sin \omega t$ Then $a=-\omega^2 A \sin \omega t$

$a = -\omega^2 x$

  • The graph between acceleration and displacement is straight line.
  • Relation between force(F) and time(t) $F = ma = -m \omega^2 A \sin(\omega t)$
Relation between force(F) and displacement(x) is $F = -m \omega^2 x$

Note:

(1)The acceleration of a particle executing S.H.M. is always directed towards the mean position.

(2) The acceleration of the particle executing S.H.M. is maximum at extreme position ($\pm \omega^2 A$) and minimum at mean position (= zero).

(3) Maximum value of acceleration is $\pm \omega^2 A$

(4) Maximum value of force is $\pm m \omega^2 A$

Key Points

Velocity and acceleration of particle in SHM :-

Displacement:
$x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi)$
$$Velocity:
$v(t) = -A \omega \sin(\omega t + \phi)$

$v = \pm \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$  (Velocity in terms of displacement)

(i) at x = 0 (mean position)     $v_{\text{max}} =\pm \omega A$

(ii) at extreme position ($x = \pm A$)      $v_{\text{min}} = 0$$$

Acceleration:
$a(t) = -A \omega^2 \cos(\omega t + \phi)$

$a = -\omega^2 x$   (Acceleration in terms of displacement)

(i) at x = 0 (Mean position)  $a_{\text{min}} = 0$

(ii) at Extreme position   ($x = \pm A$)    $a = \pm \omega^2 A$

Phase difference between x, v and a :

  • (i) displacement and velocity = $\frac{\pi}{2}$
  • (ii) velocity and acceleration =$\frac{\pi}{2}$
  • (iii) displacement and acceleration = $\pi
$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Potential Energy in S.H.M.

(1) In terms of displacement

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 + C$

$\text{At } x = 0, \, U = U_0 \Rightarrow C = U_0 \quad \text{So,} \quad U =\dfrac{1}{2} kx^2 + U_0$

Where the potential energy at equilibrium position = $U_0$

when $U_0 = 0$ then $U =\dfrac{1}{2} kx^2$

(2) In terms of time

$x = A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$

$U = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 \sin^2(\omega t + \phi)$

$\text{If initial phase } (\phi) \text{ is zero, then} \quad U = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 \sin^2(\omega t) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \sin^2(\omega t)$

Note:

In S.H.M. the potential energy is a parabolic function of displacement; the potential energy is minimum$\left(u=v_0\right)$ at the mean position $(x = 0)$ and maximum $(U=\frac{1}{2} k A^2+U_0)$ at extreme position $(x = \pm A)$

Kinetic Energy$(K.E.)$

(1) In terms of displacement

$\text{K.E.} = \dfrac{1}{2} mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} k (A^2 - x^2)$

(2) In terms of time

$ \text{K.E.} = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \cos^2(\omega t + \phi)$

$\text{If initial phase } \phi = 0, \quad \text{K.E.} = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \cos^2(\omega t)$

Note:

In S.H.M. the kinetic energy is a inverted parabolic function of displacement; the kinetic energy is maximum($\frac{1}{2} k A^2)$ at the mean position $(x = 0)$ and minimum (zero) at extreme position $(x = \pm A)$

Total Energy in SHM and Graphs

Total energy in S.H.M. is given by :-

E = potential energy + kinetic energy = U + K.E

(1)  w.r.t Position:

$E = \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 = \text{Constant}$

(2) w.r.t Time

$ E = \dfrac{1}{2} k A^2 = \text{Constant}$

Note:

(1)Total energy of a particle in S.H.M. is same at all instant and at all displacement.

(2)Total energy depends upon mass, amplitude and frequency of vibration of the particle executing S.H.M.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
(1) Spring Block System

(1) When spring is given small displacement by stretching or compressing it, then restoring elastic force is developed in it which obeys Hook's law.

$F \propto -x \quad \Rightarrow \quad F = -kx$ (Here $k$ is a spring constant)

(2) Spring is assumed massless, so restoring elastic force in spring is assumed same everywhere

(3) Spring constant $(k) $depends on length $(l),$radius and material of wire used in spring.

For spring,$ kl = constant$

(2) Spring Pendulum : When a small mass is suspended from a mass-less spring then this arrangement is known as spring pendulum. For small linear displacement the motion of spring pendulum is simple harmonic.

(i) Time-Period

$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

(ii) Frequency

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$

(3) Time period of a spring pendulum is independent of acceleration due to gravity. This is why a clock based on oscillation of spring pendulum will keep proper time everywhere on a hill or moon or in a satellite or different places of earth.

(4) If a spring pendulum oscillates in a vertical plane is made to oscillate on a horizontal surface or on an inclined plane then time period will remain unchanged.

(5) By increasing the mass, time period of spring pendulum increases $(T \propto \sqrt{m})$ , but by increasing the force constant of spring$ (k)$,Its time period decreases $T \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{k}}$

whereas frequency increases $f \propto \sqrt{k}$

(6) If two masses m1 and m2 are connected by a spring and made to oscillate then time period $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu}{k}}$  Here $\mu = \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$= reduced mass

(7) If the stretch in a vertically loaded spring is y0 then for equilibrium of mass m.

$k y_0 = mg$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{y_0

}{g}}$

But remember time period of spring pendulum is independent of acceleration due to gravity.

(8) If two particles are attached with spring in which only one is oscillating then the

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m_1}{k}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Simple Pendulum: If a heavy point mass is suspended by a weightless, inextensible and perfectly flexible string from a rigid support, then this arrangement is called a simple pendulum.$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$

Cases of Effective Acceleration in Simple Pendulum

Periodic time of simple pendulum in reference system

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}}$

$g_{\text{eff}} = $ effective gravitational acceleration in reference system (or total downward acceleration)

(a) If reference system is lift

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}} \quad \text{where} \quad g_{\text{eff}} = g \quad \text{when velocity of lift} \ (v) = \text{constant}, \ a = 0$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$

(b) If Lift is accelerating upwards

$g_{\text{eff}} = g + a$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g + a}}$

$T$$\Rightarrow$ Decreases

(c) If Lift is accelerating Downwards

$g_{\text{eff}} = g - a$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g - a}}$

$T$$\Rightarrow$ Increases

(d) If lift falls downwards freely

$g_{\text{eff}} = g - g$

$T=$$\infty$

simple pendulum will not oscillate.

Note: If simple pendulum is shifted to the centre of earth, freely falling lift, in artificial satellite then it will not oscillate and its time period is infinite ( geff. = 0).

blocks.title: Core concept
blocks.text:
A simple pendulum is mounted on a moving truck

• If truck is moving with constant velocity, no pseudo force acts on the pendulum and time period remains same.

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$

• If truck accelerates forward with acceleration 'a' then a pseudo force acts in opposite direction.

$T' = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{\sqrt{g^2 + a^2}}}$

$T'$$\Rightarrow$ decreases.

• If a simple pendulum of density $\sigma$ is made to oscillate in a liquid of density $\rho$ then its time period will increase as compare to that of air and is given by

$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{\left[1-\dfrac{\rho}{\sigma}\right] g}}$

• If the bob of simple pendulum has positive charge q and pendulum is placed in uniform electric field which is in downward direction then time period decreases

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g + \dfrac{qE}{m}}}$

• If the bob of simple pendulum has positive charge q and is made oscillate in uniform electric field acting in upward direction then time period increases

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g - \dfrac{qE}{m}}}$

When length of simple pendulum (l) is negligible as compare to radius of earth (l<< R) but if  is comparable to radius of earth

$ T=2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{\left[\dfrac{1}{\ell}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right] \mathrm{g}}}$

l = length of pendulum, R = radius of earth

• Second Pendulum :- On the surface of the Earth, the length of a second pendulum is approximately 1 metre and its time period is 2 seconds.

• When a long and short pendulum start oscillation simultaneously then both will be in same phase in minimum time when short pendulum complete one more oscillation compare to long pendulum.

$\mathrm{N} \sqrt{\ell_{\ell}}=(\mathrm{N}+1) \sqrt{l_{\mathrm{s}}}$

• If the bob of a simple pendulum is suspended by a metallic wire, and the wire has a linear expansion coefficient α, and the temperature changes by $d\theta$ then the effective length of the wire becomes  $l' = l \left( 1 + \alpha \, \Delta \theta \right)$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{T}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{T}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell^{\prime}}{\ell}}=(1+\alpha \mathrm{d} \theta)^{1 / 2}=1+\dfrac{1}{2} \alpha \mathrm{~d} \theta$
